title: I Took the Antiwork Spreadsheet to the All-Hands

parts.text: I walked into the all-hands with a USB stick that still had a grocery list on it. I am thirty-one, night warehouse, dry humor, bad coffee. Corporate wanted "feedback culture." Our manager, Vince, wanted quiet. He had been shaving lunch to twenty-two minutes and calling it operational excellence. I timed it on a cheap Casio that beeps if you bump it. Twelve of us logged our real lunches for three weeks in a sheet named snacks so it looked boring. The break room still smelled like burnt coffee and cardboard bananas. Vince clapped. "We're a family. Families don't clock-watch." My coworker Lila muttered, "Families don't badge you into overtime." Vince heard her. "Do you have something to share?" I stood because Lila has a kid and I have a USB. "Yes," I said. I plugged it into the demo laptop they left logged in as Admin, which is a personality test they keep failing. The snacks sheet filled the projector. Vince laughed once. "That's not official." Payroll from corporate, a woman named Gwen, leaned forward. "Those timestamps match the badge server." Vince's neck went blotchy. He said, "Delete that." I said, "It's already in their inbox." The Casio beeped in my pocket like a snitch. Then Vince announced an unscheduled safety drill and pulled the fire alarm, which is a choice you only make if you think noise can erase a spreadsheet.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: He pulled the fire alarm mid-meeting to kill the projector while payroll is staring at the badge match.

social.video_title: He called lunch theft operational excellence — Part 1/2
social.description: A Casio watch, a USB with a grocery list, and a sheet named snacks. Payroll said the timestamps matched. Would you have stood up for your coworker?

parts.text: I unplugged the USB and walked toward the exit with everyone else, because a fire alarm is still. Outside, Gwen found me by the propane cage. "Send the file to this address," she said. I already had. Vince tried to write me up for theft of proprietary data, meaning our own lunches. HR asked if I had recorded people without consent. I had logged my own times and voluntary entries. Lila's row stayed. Vince's safety-drill story died when the alarm company bill showed a manual pull. They restored thirty-eight-minute lunches, which is not generous, just legal. Vince transferred to mornings in a different building. I kept the Casio. It still beeps. The grocery list on the USB was milk, tortillas, and the good salsa. I bought them on the way home and ate in my car like a celebration that didn't need a speech. Months later a new hire asked if we were a family. I said we are a warehouse with a badge server that does not love anyone. He laughed. I showed him the break room microwave, which still burns popcorn if you look away. That is the whole culture. I can live with popcorn. I could not live with twenty-two minutes and a smile. He said, "Don't make this a scene." I said, "It already is."

social.video_title: The alarm company bill ended the drill story — Part 2/2
social.description: HR called lunches proprietary. The badge server disagreed. Would you have eaten salsa in the car afterward?
